ety.text: From Middle English wisdom, from Old English wīsdōm (“wisdom”), from Proto-West Germanic *wīsadōm, from Proto-Germanic *wīsadōmaz (“wisdom”), corresponding to wise + -dom. Cognate with Scots wisdom, wysdom (“wisdom”), West Frisian wiisdom (“wisdom”), Dutch wijsdom (“wisdom”), German Weistum (“legal sentence”), Danish/Norwegian/Swedish visdom (“wisdom”), Icelandic vísdómur (“wisdom”).

senses.d: An element of personal character that enables one to distinguish the wise from the unwise.
A piece of wise advice.
The discretionary use of knowledge for the greatest good.
The ability to apply relevant knowledge in an insightful way, especially to different situations from that in which the knowledge was gained.
The ability to make a decision based on the combination of knowledge, experience, and intuitive understanding.
The ability to know and apply spiritual truths.
A group of wombats.
A group of owls.

ety.text: From Middle English wisen (“to advise, direct”), from Old English wisian (“to show the way, guide, direct”), from Proto-West Germanic *wīsōn, from Proto-Germanic *wīsōną (“to show the way, dispense knowledge”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to know”). Compare Dutch wijzen (“to indicate, point out”), German weisen (“to show, indicate”), Danish and Norwegian Bokmål vise (“to show”), Norwegian Nynorsk visa (“to show”).

senses.d: Showing good judgement or the benefit of experience.
ex: Storing extra food for the winter was a wise decision.
They were considered the wise old men of the administration.

senses.d: Disrespectful.
ex: Don't get wise with me!

senses.d: Aware, informed (to something).
ex: Be careful: the boss is wise to your plan to call out sick.

senses.d: To become wise.
Usually with "up", to inform or learn.
ex: Mo wised him up about his situation.
After Mo had a word with him, he wised up.

senses.d: Way, manner, or method.
ex: In such wise that all the beasts, great and small, came to the court save Reynard the Fox.

[…] the prize
Dead Greece vouchsafes to living eyes, —
Her Art for ever in fresh wise
From hour to hour rejoicing me.

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French sage, from Old French sage, ultimately from the Classical Latin adjective sagāx.
Borrowed from Old French sage, itself from Vulgar Latin *sapium, from Latin sapiō (“to be wise”). Doublet of savio, sapio, and sapido. Compare Sicilian saviu.
Inherited from Old Spanish sabio, from Latin sapidus, from sapiō (“to be wise”, literally “to taste of”), from Proto-Indo-European *sap- (“to try, to research”). Doublet of sápido.
From juicio + -oso.

senses.d: A desire, hope, or longing for something or for something to happen.
ex: It is my wish that the bequest (should) be given to an almshouse.
make someone's wish come true

senses.d: An expression of such a desire, often connected with ideas of magic and supernatural power.
ex: make a wish

senses.d: The thing desired or longed for.
ex: My dearest wish is to see them happily married.
You have my best wishes.

senses.d: A water meadow.
To desire; to want.
ex: I'll come tomorrow, if you wish (it).
I wish it to be known that I wish them all to leave the company.

senses.d: To hope (+ object clause with may or in present subjunctive).
ex: She hears that Miss Bigg is to be married in a fortnight. I wish it may be so.
I wish he mean me well, that he takes so much pains!

senses.d: To hope (for a particular outcome), even if that outcome is unlikely to occur or cannot occur.
ex: I wish I could go back in time and teach myself what I know now.
I wished (that) it would rain.

senses.d: To bestow (a thought or gesture) towards (someone or something).
ex: We wish you a merry Christmas.
I wouldn't wish that on my worst enemy.

senses.d: To request or desire to do an activity.
ex: Anyone who wishes to may leave now.

senses.d: To recommend; to seek confidence or favour on behalf of.
ex: I was wished to your worship by a gentleman.
